newsitem.title: FRANCE: French investors keep nerve amid poll uncertainty.
newsitem.headline: French investors keep nerve amid poll uncertainty.

text.p: French bond investors are keeping their nerve in the face of opinion polls showing the left gaining ground in the country's parliamentary election race, still confident the ruling centre-right coalition will win.
"There is still a consensus view that the right will win," said economist Jean-Francois Mercier of Salomon Brothers.
But analysts said the market may be over-optimistic and that if polls show the left advancing convincingly ahead of the May 25-June 1 two-round vote, it could retreat rapidly.

"They are a little too hopeful," said Deutsche Bank economist Patrick Mange. While he said he did not expect a victory by the left, "it astonishes me that they (the market) do not seem to have taken into account that the left could win."

A win by the Socialists would trigger an initial big sell-off, economists and analysts said, but they believed the market would stabilise after it became clear that Socialist policy would not deviate much from that of the centre-right.
"The market probably assumes rightly even if the Socialists win they will remain committed to monetary union," said Mercier.

A poll by IPSOS institute released on Thursday forecast the rightist RPR/UDF coalition would get 290 seats in the National Assembly, just one more than is needed for a majority, the Socialists and their allies would win 264 and the Communists 22 for a total of 285, just four short of the RPR-UDF tally.

It was the slimmest lead yet for Prime Minister Alain Juppe's coalition since President Jacques Chirac gambled and called the election early to give him a free hand in the runup to a single European currency to pursue his austerity policies.
The poll gave the RPR-UDF taking 38 percent of the vote, the Socialists and their allies 29 percent and the Communists nine.

The market showed little reaction with the 10-year bond future up 14 basis points at 129.66 at mid-afternoon, although the negative yield premium on 10-year government bonds (OATs) over their German counterparts narrowed two basis points.

One dealer said the left often scored better in IPSOS polls than in those by other houses. "We've a lot of polls next week. If they confirm the Socialists gaining, the market will react negatively," said Paribas analyst Nathalie Fillet of Paribas.
Analysts said while short-dated debt was holding up relatively well, underperformance would become more marked in face of further market-unfriendly news.

Morgan Stanley economist Eric Chaney said the high degree of undecided in the polls made them less reliable. But if the percentage of those supporting the RPR-UDF fell to 35 percent, he would expect the market to react "pretty negatively".

The French bond market is sheltered by the small share of domestic debt in hands of outsiders, normally quick to sell at the first hint of political uncertainty. Just 12 percent of government notes and bonds are held by outsiders. The big actors are domestic financial institutions, in for the longer haul.
The French bourse, held 30 percent by foreigners, was taking the election uncertainty more on the chin, as shown by its underperformance against other European markets, traders said.
"You have got almost a 1,000 point gap between the CAC-40 index (of 40 main shares) and the (German) Dax.30," said one. "There is a lot of uncertainty already in the share prices."
The CAC-40 index was down 11.75 points or 0.44 percent at 2,632.10 at midafternoon while London pushed higher and Wall Street opened firmer.
Economists said they were already detecting a move toward the centre by the Socialists in their latest decarations.

"At the start they were talking about raising business taxes. Their new manifesto doesn't talk about that and there is obviously disagreement over privatisation policy in the party," said Deutsche Bank's Mange.

A recent poll of economists suggested an opposition win would leave the franc by June 15 more than three centimes weaker against the mark at 3.41 against 3.3740 on Friday. French 10-year bond yields would also suffer with yields expected to climb to 20 basis points above 10-year Bund yields compared with minus seven basis points on Friday. The two-year spread would snap out to 40 from 20 on Friday if the left won.
But French and German 10-year bond yields were expected to be the same by October 15 even in event of a left win.
